description: Somos DYNAMIC CODING, un equipo de Santa Cruz de la Sierra apasionado por el espacio y la programación. Elegimos el desafío “Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer”: crearemos un juego interactivo donde niños administren una base en la Luna o Marte, equilibrando energía, comida, soporte vital y radiación con datos reales de la NASA. Buscamos programadores (JavaScript/Unity/Godot), diseñadores UI/UX o de videojuegos y alguien con gusto por la ciencia o la educación. ¡Súmate a la misión! 🚀
summary:
Mission Selene-Ares is a 3D educational video game for children aged 7 to 12, developed in Godot 4 and playable via web browser or on Android. Players take on the role of an astronaut, accompanied by an android co-pilot named A.R.T.I., as they embark on a full-scale journey: preparing rocket cargo on Earth, landing on the Moon, managing a lunar biodome, working at a station in lunar orbit, and finally reaching Mars.

The game incorporates real, open-source NASA data into the adventure: the strongest solar flare from the past month (via the DONKI database) determines the solar storm the player must withstand; asteroids identified for the day (via the NeoWs service) appear during the journey; and a study from the OSDR (Open Science Data Repository) informs the astronaut’s medical check-up. The game always indicates whether the data being used is live or archived.

This project is significant because it makes space science accessible and relatable. Children learn through play—without penalties for making mistakes—and discover that NASA’s data is within reach for everyone.
details:
What is it and how does it work?

Mission Selene-Ares is a 3D first-person game in which the player takes on the role of an astronaut traveling from Earth to the Moon, and subsequently to Mars. The player is accompanied by A.R.T.I., an android co-pilot who provides guidance for each step through both voice and text. The journey includes several missions: selecting the rocket’s payload and launching from Earth; landing the lunar module on the Moon; maintaining a biodome and surviving a solar storm; operating a rover remotely from the Aurora station in lunar orbit; and, finally, exploring Mars.

The game integrates with NASA’s open data:

DONKI: The strongest solar flare from the last 30 days determines the intensity of the solar storm the player must face.

NeoWs: Near-Earth asteroids identified for that specific day appear during the journey to the Moon.

OSDR (study OSD-575): This informs the astronaut’s medical check-up upon waking in lunar orbit.

Each data point is labeled according to its source: “live,” “archived,” or “practice event.” No data is ever presented as real if it is fictional.

Benefits

Children learn real-world concepts—such as varying gravity on different worlds, space weather, limited resources, and health in space—through play rather than rote memorization. Making mistakes is never penalized; if a resource runs out, A.R.T.I. provides a reserve and explains what happened, keeping the player motivated and turning errors into learning opportunities.

Expected Impact

The project aims to introduce space science and NASA’s open data to Spanish-speaking children aged 7 to 12, helping to spark an interest in scientific careers. Because it runs in a web browser and on Android, it can be used in schools and at home without the need for expensive equipment or complex installations.

Tools and Technologies

Godot 4.7 engine using the GDScript language.

Compatibility renderer (OpenGL/WebGL) to enable web-based execution. NASA APIs: DONKI, NeoWs, and OSDR.

3D models in glTF format with custom shaders.

Exported for Web (HTML5) and Android, featuring touch controls.

Git and GitHub used for team collaboration.

Creativity

Real NASA data isn’t just displayed in a table—it shapes the gameplay. A solar storm in the game today reflects what the Sun actually did this month. Landscapes of Earth, the Moon, and Mars are procedurally generated in a low-poly, flat-color style, while a voiced character guides the player through the story.

Key Considerations

Target Audience: Simple language, a clear color-coding system (turquoise for "safe to interact with," red reserved for emergencies), and no penalties for losing.

Accessibility: Designed to run in web browsers and on entry-level mobile devices; we prioritized performance optimization and kept model file sizes small.

Scientific Integrity: The source of every piece of data is clearly cited, and archived copies are included so the game can function offline.

Licensing: We document the author and license for every third-party asset used.
